# Date the Ad — Full Content Script

Every ad, note, episode link, and quote in the game.

**Generated file — do not edit by hand.** Edit the data in `index.html`, then run
`node build-content-doc.js` to regenerate this.

**36 ads** in the pool · **23** link to episodes · **7** score on the vintage curve · **22** rotating footer quotes

Span: 1886–2013. Ten are drawn at random per playthrough.

---

## The ads

Listed chronologically. Vintage ads (pre-1926) score on the wider curve.

### 1886 — Pears' Soap — “Bubbles”

*Image · Vintage scoring*

**Why it matters.** The moment advertising discovered fine art. Buying a Royal Academy painting to sell soap scandalized critics — and set the template for a century of aspirational brand imagery.

**Did you know?** Millais painted his own grandson; the Illustrated London News then sold the copyright to Pears, who added the bar of soap. He was reportedly furious at first, and came round on seeing the proof.

**Source.** [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Bubbles_by_John_Everett_Millais.jpg)

### 1888 — Kodak — “You Press the Button, We Do the Rest”

*Image · Vintage scoring*

**Why it matters.** One of the first great advertising slogans — a promise of simplicity that sold a technology by hiding it. Every 'it just works' pitch since owes it a debt.

**Did you know?** George Eastman wrote the slogan himself to launch the first Kodak camera. It turned photography from a chemist's hobby into a mass-market pastime almost overnight.

**Source.** [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:You_press_the_button,_we_do_the_rest_(Kodak).jpg)

### 1898 — Michelin — “Nunc est Bibendum”

*Image · Vintage scoring*

**Why it matters.** The birth of the brand mascot. Bibendum proved a company could be embodied by a character — decades before Tony the Tiger or Ronald McDonald existed.

**Did you know?** O'Galop's poster shows the Michelin Man toasting with a glass of nails and shards, because Michelin tires “drink up obstacles.” He's one of the oldest mascots still working.

**Source.** [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Michelin_Poster_1898.jpg)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Giana Eckhardt: The Origins of Branding in Imperial China](https://marketinghistory.org/p/giana-eckhardt-origins-of-branding-china)
  <br>on Bibendum as the first brand mascot, and where branding really began

### 1900 — Coca-Cola — “Delicious and Refreshing”

*Image · Vintage scoring*

**Why it matters.** Among the first celebrity endorsements in American advertising — establishing the playbook of borrowing fame to build a brand that the industry still runs on.

**Did you know?** Music-hall star Hilda Clark was Coca-Cola's first celebrity endorser. At the time a glass cost five cents at the soda fountain — a price Coke famously held for over 70 years.

**Source.** [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cocacola-5cents-1900_edit1.jpg)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Richard S. Tedlow: The Story of Mass Marketing in America](https://marketinghistory.org/p/richard-s-tedlow-mass-marketing-in-america)
  <br>the rise of mass marketing in America, and the Cola Wars it produced

### 1905 — Clark Stanley — Snake Oil Liniment

*Image · Vintage scoring*

**Why it matters.** The ad that named a whole genre of deception. Patent-medicine hype like Stanley's is why “snake oil salesman” means what it means — and why ad regulation exists.

**Did you know?** By 1916 federal chemists had found the liniment contained no snake oil at all. Stanley was fined $20, and truth-in-advertising law followed the era's abuses.

**Source.** [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Clark_Stanley%27s_Snake_Oil_Liniment.png)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Mark Tungate: Advertising History from Ancient Pompeii to Today](https://marketinghistory.org/p/mark-tungate-advertising-history)
  <br>on the patent-medicine era that gave advertising its bad name

### 1917 — U.S. Army — “I Want YOU” (Uncle Sam)

*Image · Vintage scoring*

**Why it matters.** Propaganda as direct-response advertising. The pointing finger and the word “YOU” made the viewer the audience of one — among the most imitated compositions in poster history.

**Did you know?** James Montgomery Flagg used his own face (aged up, with a goatee) as the model for Uncle Sam. Over four million copies were printed during World War I.

**Source.** [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Unclesamwantyou.jpg)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Larry Tye on Edward Bernays: “The Father of Public Relations”](https://marketinghistory.org/p/larry-tye-on-edward-bernays-the-father)
  <br>how wartime propaganda became the public relations industry

### 1917 — Lucky Strike — “It's Toasted”

*Image · Vintage scoring*

**Why it matters.** The “reason why” school in three words: every maker toasted its tobacco, but Lucky Strike claimed the process first — a move marketers still copy.

**Did you know?** Mad Men opens with Don Draper dreaming up “It's toasted” in 1960 — a great scene, and four decades late. Lucky Strike had been running the line since the First World War.

**Source.** [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lucky_strike_it%27s_toasted.jpg)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Larry Tye on Edward Bernays: “The Father of Public Relations”](https://marketinghistory.org/p/larry-tye-on-edward-bernays-the-father)
  <br>how Bernays sold cigarettes to women as “torches of freedom”

### 1943 — Westinghouse — “We Can Do It!” (Rosie the Riveter)

*Image*

**Why it matters.** Wartime internal propaganda turned feminist icon: made to boost factory morale, rediscovered decades later as shorthand for women's economic power.

**Did you know?** J. Howard Miller's poster hung in Westinghouse plants for just two weeks. It only became “Rosie the Riveter” when the 1980s rediscovered it.

**Source.** [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:We_Can_Do_It!.jpg)

### 1955 — Marlboro — The Marlboro Man

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** The most effective rebrand in history: Leo Burnett took a “mild as May” cigarette marketed to women and made it the best-selling brand on earth with one cowboy.

**Did you know?** Within two years of the cowboy's debut, Marlboro's US sales had multiplied more than tenfold. The imagery ran until tobacco left the airwaves.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N6xa30WYgT4)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Jean Kilbourne: “Killing Us Softly” & Pioneering Feminist Advertising Criticism](https://marketinghistory.org/p/jean-kilbourne-killing-us-softly)
  <br>the critic who spent a career taking aim at how tobacco advertised

### 1959 — Volkswagen — “Think Small”

*Image*

**Why it matters.** Ad Age's #1 campaign of the century. DDB's honest, witty minimalism launched the Creative Revolution and taught advertising to treat readers as intelligent.

**Did you know?** Bill Bernbach's great innovation was pairing copywriters with art directors — a partnership that produced this ad's acres of white space and self-deprecating wit.

**Source.** [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Think_Small.jpg)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Mark Tungate: Advertising History from Ancient Pompeii to Today](https://marketinghistory.org/p/mark-tungate-advertising-history)
  <br>on Bill Bernbach and the Creative Revolution this ad set off

### 1960 — Xerox — 914 Copier (Sam the Chimpanzee)

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** Demonstration advertising at its cheekiest: if a chimpanzee can make a copy, anyone can. It sold a machine by selling effortlessness.

**Did you know?** The Xerox 914 became so dominant that “to xerox” entered the language as a verb — a trademark lawyer's nightmare, a marketer's dream.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hkEykPawTrg)

### 1971 — Coca-Cola — “Hilltop” (I'd Like to Buy the World a Coke)

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** The high-water mark of advertising idealism — selling a soft drink as world peace. It proved a commercial could jump the fence into pop culture and live there.

**Did you know?** Shot on a hillside in Italy after the original airfield shoot was rained out, the jingle was re-recorded as “I'd Like to Teach the World to Sing” and became a genuine chart hit — twice.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1VM2eLhvsSM)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Sergio Zyman, Part 1: “The First Chief Marketing Officer”](https://marketinghistory.org/p/sergio-zyman-the-first-chief-marketing-officer)
  <br>Coca-Cola's first Chief Marketing Officer on building the brand
- [Sergio Zyman, Part 2: New Coke and “The End of Marketing as We Know It”](https://marketinghistory.org/p/sergio-zyman-part-2-new-coke-end-of-marketing)
  <br>and on New Coke, the decision that tested everything Hilltop stood for

### 1977 — New York State — “I ❤ NY”

*Image · Light background*

**Why it matters.** Place branding's masterpiece: Milton Glaser's logo, made for a bankrupt, crime-ridden city, became the most imitated tourism mark on earth.

**Did you know?** Glaser sketched the concept on scrap paper in a taxi — the sketch is now in MoMA — and did the work pro bono, expecting it to run a few months.

**Source.** [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:I_Love_New_York.svg)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Mark Tungate: Advertising History from Ancient Pompeii to Today](https://marketinghistory.org/p/mark-tungate-advertising-history)
  <br>on Mary Wells Lawrence and the New York agency scene behind the campaign

### 1979 — Coca-Cola — “Hey Kid, Catch!” (Mean Joe Greene)

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** The template for emotional sports marketing: a 60-second story with no product claim — just human warmth between a weary hero and a kid with a Coke.

**Did you know?** The shoot took three days and dozens of Cokes. It first aired on Monday Night Football — the Super Bowl broadcast everyone remembers came months later.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xffOCZYX6F8)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Sergio Zyman, Part 1: “The First Chief Marketing Officer”](https://marketinghistory.org/p/sergio-zyman-the-first-chief-marketing-officer)
  <br>Coca-Cola's first Chief Marketing Officer on the era that produced this ad
- [Sergio Zyman, Part 2: New Coke and “The End of Marketing as We Know It”](https://marketinghistory.org/p/sergio-zyman-part-2-new-coke-end-of-marketing)
  <br>and on New Coke, the misstep that followed

### 1983 — British Airways — “Manhattan”

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** Saatchi & Saatchi's spectacle for “the world's favourite airline”: flying Manhattan island across the Atlantic, with Hollywood effects no airline ad had attempted.

**Did you know?** The premise: BA flies more people across the Atlantic every year than the entire population of Manhattan.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vZu0y-D6BMs)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Mark Tungate: Advertising History from Ancient Pompeii to Today](https://marketinghistory.org/p/mark-tungate-advertising-history)
  <br>on Saatchi & Saatchi and how this ad got made

### 1984 — Apple — “Big Brother” Macintosh launch

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** The Super Bowl ad as cultural event begins here. A product launch staged as dystopian cinema, it positioned the Mac not as a computer but as a creative tool.

**Did you know?** Directed by Ridley Scott fresh off Blade Runner, the Orwell-inspired spot aired nationally just once — and people still talk about it every February.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VtvjbmoDx-I)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Tim Calkins: Why Super Bowl Ads Are Still Worth It](https://marketinghistory.org/p/tim-calkins-super-bowl-ads)
  <br>how one spot turned the Super Bowl into advertising's main stage
- [Mark Tungate: Advertising History from Ancient Pompeii to Today](https://marketinghistory.org/p/mark-tungate-advertising-history)
  <br>on the agencies and ideas that shaped the modern industry

### 1984 — Wendy's — “Where's the Beef?”

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** Proof a catchphrase could escape the ad break entirely — it jumped into the presidential race when Walter Mondale aimed it at a rival in a debate.

**Did you know?** Clara Peller was an 81-year-old retired manicurist when she was cast. Wendy's sales jumped roughly 30% in the year the ad ran.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U80ebi4AKgs)

### 1985 — Levi's — “Laundrette”

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** British advertising's pop-culture breakthrough: BBH sold jeans as cinema, lifted 501 sales roughly 800%, and sent its sixties soundtrack back up the charts.

**Did you know?** Nick Kamen stripping to his boxers to Marvin Gaye's “I Heard It Through the Grapevine” also triggered a national run on boxer shorts.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mKa_uQCz3Hw)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Tracey Panek: Levi's Corporate Historian on Building a Timeless Brand](https://marketinghistory.org/p/tracey-panek-levis-corporate-historian)
  <br>Levi's own historian on how the brand built its mythology

### 1988 — Nike — “Just Do It” (first commercial)

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** Three words that turned a running-shoe company into a philosophy. The campaign made the brand — not the product — the hero, and modern sports marketing followed.

**Did you know?** The first “Just Do It” spot starred 80-year-old runner Walt Stack jogging across the Golden Gate Bridge. Dan Wieden coined the slogan partly inspired — grimly — by a convicted murderer's last words.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0yO7xLAGugQ)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Scott Reames: Nike's First-ever Historian Shares Secrets Behind the Swoosh](https://marketinghistory.org/p/scott-reames-nike-historian)
  <br>Nike's first-ever historian on the secrets behind the Swoosh

### 1991–1997 — Barclaycard — Rowan Atkinson

*Video · Campaign span · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** A rare case of a brand selling itself through its own uselessness in the wrong hands. Atkinson's bungling agent got the card's benefits wrong for six years, and viewers learned them anyway.

**Did you know?** Atkinson's hapless spy Richard Latham was the prototype for Johnny English, who a decade later graduated into his own film trilogy.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RylTP_5fG0s)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Paul Feldwick: “The only honest case study in the history of marketing”](https://marketinghistory.org/p/paul-feldwick-barclaycard-case-study)
  <br>Paul Feldwick on why this is “the only honest case study in the history of marketing”

### 1993 — Got Milk? — “Aaron Burr”

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** The deprivation strategy in one spot: sell the product by imagining its absence. It launched one of America's longest-running campaigns.

**Did you know?** A young Michael Bay directed it for Goodby Silverstein: a peanut-butter-mouthed history buff who can't say “Aaron Burr” loses a $10,000 radio quiz.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0Gkqzxss8Ss)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Paul Feldwick: Deconstructing the Myths of Advertising](https://marketinghistory.org/p/paul-feldwick-deconstructing-advertising-myths)
  <br>on advertising's real power to mint catchphrases and build fame

### 1997 — Apple — “Think Different” (Here's to the Crazy Ones)

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** Apple's comeback manifesto. Aired weeks after Steve Jobs returned, it rebuilt the brand as a creative tool for rebels — the positioning Apple trades on to this day.

**Did you know?** Richard Dreyfuss narrated the broadcast version, but a cut voiced by Jobs himself exists — he decided at the last minute it shouldn't be about him.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5sMBhDv4sik)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Guy Kawasaki: The Remarkable Rise of Evangelism Marketing](https://marketinghistory.org/p/guy-kawasaki-the-remarkable-rise)
  <br>Apple's former chief evangelist on building the faithful

### 1997 — Taco Bell — “Yo Quiero Taco Bell” (Chihuahua)

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** A talking dog became a national catchphrase — and later a cautionary tale about mascots whose fame outruns the sales they're meant to drive.

**Did you know?** Gidget, the female Chihuahua who played the male dog, got a movie cameo out of it. The campaign ended when sales lagged behind the fame.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aKLW0kQ83qg)

### 1999 — Budweiser — “Whassup?!”

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** An early viral phenomenon — proof a catchphrase could carry a brand across talk shows, playgrounds, and the early internet without a single product claim.

**Did you know?** Adapted from Charles Stone III's short film 'True' and starring his real friends, “Whassup?!” won the Cannes Grand Prix and entered everyday speech.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JJmqCKtJnxM)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Tim Calkins: Why Super Bowl Ads Are Still Worth It](https://marketinghistory.org/p/tim-calkins-super-bowl-ads)
  <br>six decades of Super Bowl advertising, and what the money buys

### 1999 — Guinness — “Surfer”

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** “Good things come to those who wait” turned a slow pour into mythology — white horses in the surf, routinely voted the best British ad ever made.

**Did you know?** AMV BBDO's voiceover channels Moby-Dick's Ahab; real big-wave surfers were blended with CGI horses over Leftfield's “Phat Planet.”

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rE1lIdtDs2g)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [David Gluckman: Why the Inventor of Baileys Thinks Market Research is Bullsh*t](https://marketinghistory.org/p/david-gluckman-inventor-of-baileys)
  <br>the man who invented Baileys on how drinks brands are really built

### 1999 — Nintendo — Super Smash Bros. “Happy Together”

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** Nintendo sold a fighting game as absurdist comedy — beloved mascots brawling in a meadow to “Happy Together” — a tone the franchise still uses.

**Did you know?** The costumed Mario, Yoshi, Pikachu, and DK shoot launched an N64 series that became Nintendo's best-selling crossover juggernaut.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K783SDTBKmg)

### 2002 — IKEA — “Lamp”

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** Anti-sentimentality as strategy: Spike Jonze made viewers mourn a discarded lamp, then punctured the emotion to sell “new and better.” Won the Cannes Grand Prix.

**Did you know?** The Swedish man who scolds you — “you're crazy, it has no feelings” — delivered the twist standing in fake Los Angeles rain.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jU-cori12KU)

### 2003 — Honda — “Cog”

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** Two minutes, 85 Accord parts, one unbroken chain reaction, no CGI — craft itself became the selling point, and the internet did the media buy.

**Did you know?** It took 606 takes. Too long for most TV slots, it spread online instead — an early sign that great ads no longer needed airtime.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w4XiaP-WhNw)

### 2006 — Apple — “Get a Mac” (I'm a Mac)

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** Positioning as sitcom: 66 spots that personified two computers and made the competitor the punchline without citing a single spec.

**Did you know?** Justin Long played Mac, John Hodgman played PC. Adweek later named it the best campaign of the decade.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=48jlm6QSU4k)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Guy Kawasaki: The Remarkable Rise of Evangelism Marketing](https://marketinghistory.org/p/guy-kawasaki-the-remarkable-rise)
  <br>Apple's former chief evangelist on turning customers into believers

### 2006 — Dove — “Evolution”

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** The film that launched the purpose era: a time-lapse from model to billboard exposed manufactured beauty and made media literacy a brand platform.

**Did you know?** Made by Ogilvy Toronto on a shoestring, it earned an estimated 500 times its budget in free media and won two Grand Prix at Cannes.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DCNEIwxkPlc)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [David Aaker: “The Father of Modern Branding” Returns](https://marketinghistory.org/p/david-aaker-the-father-of-branding-returns)
  <br>why Real Beauty is a case study in revitalizing a brand
- [Nick Asbury: The Case Against “Purpose”](https://marketinghistory.org/p/nick-asbury-the-case-against-purpose)
  <br>the counterargument: how purpose made every brand sound the same

### 2010 — Old Spice — “The Man Your Man Could Smell Like”

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** The ad that cracked the social-media era: made for TV, engineered for YouTube, and willing to answer its audience back in real time.

**Did you know?** Isaiah Mustafa's single-take monologue (horse included) debuted online before the Super Bowl. The follow-up campaign — 186 personalized YouTube replies filmed in two days — helped define social marketing.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=owGykVbfgUE)

### 2010 — Snickers — “You're Not You When You're Hungry”

*Video · Title hidden*

**Why it matters.** The modern global platform: one insight — hunger changes you — translated into more than 80 markets from a single Super Bowl debut.

**Did you know?** The Betty White spot launched the campaign. Fans then petitioned for White to host SNL, which she did months later at age 88.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GkAnLtqWDhc)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Tim Calkins: Why Super Bowl Ads Are Still Worth It](https://marketinghistory.org/p/tim-calkins-super-bowl-ads)
  <br>the strategy and economics behind the Super Bowl spot

### 2010 — Google — “Parisian Love”

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** Google's first Super Bowl ad, and proof that a product demo could be a love story. The entire romance plays out in nothing but a search box.

**Did you know?** No faces, no voices, no music swell until the end — just queries typed one after another. Google had reportedly resisted TV advertising for years before running it.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nnsSUqgkDwU)

**Hear more on A History of Marketing.**

- [Tim Calkins: Why Super Bowl Ads Are Still Worth It](https://marketinghistory.org/p/tim-calkins-super-bowl-ads)
  <br>how the Super Bowl became the stage even Google couldn't resist

### 2012 — Dollar Shave Club — “Our Blades Are F***ing Great”

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** The $4,500 video that helped topple a giant: direct-to-consumer swagger with the founder as star and a punchline every five seconds.

**Did you know?** Michael Dubin wrote and starred; the site crashed within an hour of launch. Unilever later bought the company for a reported $1 billion.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZUG9qYTJMsI)

### 2012 — Metro Trains — “Dumb Ways to Die”

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** Public-safety messaging reinvented as a pop song — morbid, adorable, and the most-awarded campaign in Cannes Lions history.

**Did you know?** Made for Melbourne's Metro Trains, the song charted on iTunes in 28 countries and the spin-off game passed 100 million downloads.

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJNR2EpS0jw)

### 2013 — Volvo Trucks — “The Epic Split”

*Video · Title shown*

**Why it matters.** The B2B ad that went pop: a steering-precision demo for truck buyers became one of the most-shared ads ever made.

**Did you know?** Jean-Claude Van Damme performed the split for real between two reversing trucks, shot in one take at dawn to Enya's “Only Time.”

**Source.** [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=M7FIvfx5J10)

| [David Aaker: “The Father of Modern Branding” Returns](https://marketinghistory.org/p/david-aaker-the-father-of-branding-returns) | Dove — “Evolution” (2006) |

- “Advertising isn't a science. It's persuasion. And persuasion is an art.” — **Bill Bernbach**

- “Make it simple. Make it memorable. Make it inviting to look at.” — **Leo Burnett**

## Scoring

| Points | Modern (1926–present) | Vintage (pre-1926) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | exact | exact |
| 9 | 1 year off | 1–2 years off |
| 8 | 2 years off | 3–4 years off |
| 7 | 3 years off | 5–6 years off |
| 6 | 4 years off | 7–8 years off |
| 5 | 5 years off | 9–10 years off |
| 3 | 6–9 years off | 11–13 years off |
| 2 | 10–12 years off | 14–16 years off |
| 1 | 13–15 years off | 17–20 years off |
| 0 | more than 15 | more than 20 |

The vintage cutoff is computed as `currentYear - 100`, so it moves with time.

### Campaign ads

A few ads ran as campaigns rather than debuting once, so any year inside the span scores
the full 10, with a steeper drop-off outside it: 1 year out = 8, 2–3 = 6, 4–5 = 2, beyond = 0.

- **Barclaycard — Rowan Atkinson** — 1991–1997

## Interface copy

| Where | Text |
| --- | --- |
| Wordmark | DATE THE AD |
| Tagline | A Marketing History Game |
| Headline | Can you guess the year of the *iconic ad*? |
| Subhead | We show you a historic advertisement, from Victorian soap posters to viral Super Bowl spots. You guess the year it ran. |
| Start button | Start the Quiz |
| Round prompt | What year did this ad first run? |
| Input modes | Enter Year / Multiple Choice |
| Submit button | Rotates: Lock It In · That's My Guess · Final Answer · Ship It |
| Video guard | Title hidden |
| Media caption | Television commercial / Print advertisement · Source: … |
| Vintage popover | This ad is over a century old, so it scores on a gentler curve: exact = 10, within 2 years = 9, 4 = 8, 6 = 7, 8 = 6, 10 = 5, 13 = 3, 16 = 2, 20 = 1. Newer ads use tighter margins. |
| Campaign popover | This campaign ran for years rather than debuting once, so any year in the span scores the full 10. From there: 1 year out = 8, 2–3 = 6, 4–5 = 2. |
| Next button | Next Round → / See Final Score → |
| End screen | Share Your Score · Play Again · Share on X · Facebook · LinkedIn · Download scorecard |
| Footer | Media links to Wikimedia or YouTube source pages · From marketinghistory.org |
